code.title: Collection hierarchy and the Map views

followUps: Collection is an interface; Collections is a utility class. Collection<E> is the root type of List, Set and Queue. Collections (with an s) is a final class of static helpers such as sort, reverse, unmodifiableList, emptyList, max and synchronizedMap. Example: Collections.sort(list) works on any List, but you never create a Collections object. Similar pairs: Arrays vs array, Objects vs Object.

LinkedList implements both List and Deque. Its full list is List, Deque (and so Queue), Cloneable and Serializable; it extends AbstractSequentialList. That is why it has get(i) and also addFirst, pollLast and push. It does not implement RandomAccess, which tells algorithms that index access is slow. One class gives you list, queue and stack behaviour, but ArrayList or ArrayDeque is usually faster for each single job.

Java 21 added SequencedCollection, SequencedSet and SequencedMap for collections with a defined encounter order. They add getFirst(), getLast(), addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast and reversed(). List, Deque, LinkedHashSet and SortedSet are sequenced; LinkedHashMap and SortedMap are SequencedMap. Before 21 the last element of a list was list.get(list.size() - 1); now it is list.getLast(). HashSet is not sequenced, because it has no order.

code.title: ArrayList and LinkedList give the same result, different cost

followUps: ArrayList grows by about 1.5 times when it is full. The first add allocates 10 slots. When size equals capacity, it creates a new array of old + (old >> 1) and copies the old elements with System.arraycopy. Example: capacity 10 becomes 15, then 22, then 33. One growth costs O(n), but it happens rarely, so the average cost per add stays O(1). If you know the final size, new ArrayList<>(n) avoids every copy.

Because for-each uses an iterator that moves from node to node, while get(i) walks from the end each time. Each list.get(i) on a LinkedList costs up to n/2 steps, so a loop of n calls costs about n²/4 steps. For 100,000 elements that is billions of hops, while for-each does 100,000. The iterator keeps a pointer to the current node and just follows the next link. Rule: on a LinkedList never loop by index.

RandomAccess is a marker interface (no methods) that says get(i) is fast. ArrayList and Vector implement it; LinkedList does not. Algorithms check list instanceof RandomAccess and pick an index loop for fast lists, or an iterator for slow ones. Collections.binarySearch does this. You can use the same check in your own generic code. It documents the cost promise: constant-time positional access.

code.title: HashSet, LinkedHashSet and TreeSet on the same input

followUps: The set may treat two elements as equal that equals() says are different, so elements disappear. TreeSet uses only the comparator (or compareTo) to detect duplicates, never equals. Example: a comparator that compares strings by length makes "cat" and "dog" equal (both 3), so adding "dog" after "cat" is silently ignored and the set has size 1. This breaks the Set contract, which is defined with equals. Fix: make the comparator consistent with equals, or add a tie-breaker such as thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder()).

Because the hash decides which bucket the element lives in, and a changed field changes the hash. Example: a Point(1,2) is added and lands in bucket 5. If you later set x = 9, its hash now points to another bucket. contains(point) looks in the wrong bucket and returns false, yet the element is still stored (a leak) and shows up when you iterate. Use immutable elements such as records, Strings or Integers, or never mutate fields used in equals and hashCode while the object is in the set.

code.title: Fail-fast iterator: CME, the silent skip and safe removal

followUps: Yes, it happens in single-threaded code all the time. CME is not about threads; it is about modifying a collection while an iterator is open. Example: for (x : list) list.remove(x) on one thread throws it. list.set(i, v) inside for-each does not throw, because set is not a structural change (size does not change, modCount stays the same). Only add, remove and clear do.

Fail-fast iterators throw as soon as they notice a change; fail-safe iterators work on a copy; weakly consistent ones work on the live data and never throw. ArrayList and HashMap are fail-fast (they throw CME on a best-effort basis). CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates over a snapshot, so it never sees later changes. ConcurrentHashMap iterators are weakly consistent: they may or may not show changes made after they were created, but never throw. Choose by the need: detect bugs, stable view, or live concurrent view.

No, set() inside for-each does not throw ConcurrentModificationException. The check compares modCount, and ArrayList.set only replaces an element without changing the size, so modCount is not touched. Example: for (int i : list) list.set(0, 99); runs fine. Only structural changes (add, remove, clear, sort in some classes) bump modCount. Note: ArrayList.sort does bump it, so sorting inside for-each throws.

code.title: equals and hashCode decide the HashMap bucket

followUps: It stores the entry in a bucket that the object's other hash code does not point to, so lookups usually miss. Two equal objects get different identity hash codes, so map.get(new Key(1)) goes to another bucket and returns null even though an equal key exists (the demo above shows exactly this). Sometimes it works by luck, when both land in the same bucket, which makes the bug hard to find. Rule: override equals and hashCode together, using the same fields.

So the index can be computed with one fast AND instead of a slow modulo. With capacity 16, hash & 15 keeps the low 4 bits, equal to hash % 16 but cheaper. Power-of-two sizes also make resizing easy: when the table doubles, each entry either stays at index i or moves to i + oldCapacity, depending on one extra bit. The price is that only low bits matter, so HashMap mixes high bits into low bits with h ^ (h >>> 16).

It turns long collision chains into balanced trees. If a bucket holds 8 or more entries and the table has at least 64 slots, the chain becomes a red-black tree, so a lookup costs O(log n) instead of O(n). An attacker who sends many keys with the same hash can no longer make each lookup linear: 10,000 colliding keys cost about 14 comparisons each, not 10,000. Keys that implement Comparable get ordered inside the tree. The bit-spreading step also helps with poor hash functions.

code.title: getOrDefault, merge, computeIfAbsent and putIfAbsent

followUps: It builds a new ArrayList every time, even when the key already exists, and then throws it away. Java evaluates the argument before the call. Example: for 1,000,000 puts where the key is usually present, you allocate 1,000,000 unused lists. Use computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new ArrayList<>()), whose lambda runs only when the key is missing. Also, putIfAbsent returns the old value or null, so you cannot chain .add(...) on it without a null check.

On HashMap it can throw ConcurrentModificationException (Java 9+) or corrupt the map; on ConcurrentHashMap it can deadlock or throw IllegalStateException ("Recursive update"). The mapping function must not touch the map being computed. Example: a recursive Fibonacci memo with memo.computeIfAbsent(n, k -> fib(k - 1) + fib(k - 2)) fails for this reason. Fix: check with get first, compute outside, then put, or use an explicit loop.

code.title: PriorityQueue as min-heap, max-heap and by priority

followUps:
Keep a min-heap of size k and drop the smallest when it grows past k. For each of n items: pq.offer(x); if (pq.size() > k) pq.poll();. Each step is O(log k), so the total is O(n log k) time and O(k) space, without sorting everything. Example: for the stream 5, 1, 9, 3, 7 with k = 2, the heap ends as {7, 9}. Memory stays small even if the stream is huge.

PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
for (int x : stream) {
    pq.offer(x);
    if (pq.size() > k) pq.poll();
}

Java's PriorityQueue has no decrease-key, so you insert a new entry with the better distance and skip stale ones when polled (lazy deletion). Each edge relaxation does pq.offer(new int[]{node, newDist}). When polling, ignore entries where dist > best[node]. The queue may hold up to E entries, so the cost is O((V + E) log E) time. The alternative, pq.remove(obj), is O(n) and slower.

int[] cur = pq.poll();
if (cur[1] > best[cur[0]]) continue; // stale
// relax neighbours, offer new entries

code.title: ArrayDeque versus Stack and null handling

followUps: push and pop work at the head; offer and poll work at the tail and head, and differ in how they fail. push(x) is addFirst and pop() is removeFirst, so they form a stack. offer(x) is offerLast and poll() is pollFirst, so they form a queue. On an empty deque, pop() throws NoSuchElementException but poll() returns null. Example: push 1, 2, 3 then pop gives 3; offer 1, 2, 3 then poll gives 1.

It doubles its circular array when it is full. Its array length is a power of two. When head and tail meet, it allocates an array of twice the size (small arrays double, big ones grow by 50 percent) and copies the elements in order. Because the array is circular, indexes wrap using & (length - 1). As with ArrayList the growth cost is amortised O(1) per add.

code.title: unmodifiableList, copyOf, List.of and Arrays.asList

followUps: No, an unmodifiable wrapper is not thread-safe; it only blocks writes through the wrapper. The wrapper just forwards reads to the original list. If another thread changes the original while you read, you may see half-done changes, stale values or an exception. Example: thread A iterates a view while thread B calls src.add(5), which can throw ConcurrentModificationException. Real immutable collections (List.of, List.copyOf) are safe to share, because nobody can change them.

Because int[] is an object and a primitive array cannot be a generic type argument. Arrays.asList(T... a) needs a reference type. Passing an int[] makes the whole array one element, so T is int[] and the list has size 1 (see the demo). With Integer[] it works as expected. For primitives use Arrays.stream(arr).boxed().toList() or IntStream. This is a common interview trap.

code.title: TreeMap floor, ceiling and range views

followUps: Use TreeMap.subMap and its size, or keep a sorted timestamp list and binary search. subMap(from, true, to, true).size() builds a live view in O(log n), but calling size() on that view walks the entries, so counting is O(k) for k results. For a pure count in O(log n), store sorted timestamps in an array and take two binary searches: upperBound(to) - lowerBound(from). Example: timestamps 10..50, range [20, 40] gives index 4 minus index 1 = 3. A Fenwick tree works when updates are frequent.

Because a TreeMap has to compare keys to find a position, and null cannot be compared. With natural ordering it calls key.compareTo(other), which throws NullPointerException on null. A custom comparator could handle null (for example Comparator.nullsFirst), and then TreeMap accepts it. HashMap allows one null key because hashing null is defined as 0 and no comparison is needed. Ordered structures need a total order, and null has no natural place in it.

code.title: LRU cache with an access-order LinkedHashMap

followUps: Wrap the map in a lock, with synchronized methods or a ReentrantLock. The simplest correct version is Collections.synchronizedMap(new LRU<>(cap)), which locks every call, including get, because get changes order. Throughput is limited to one thread at a time, but it is correct. Compound steps (check then put) still need synchronized (cache) { ... }. For real load use Caffeine, which separates reads from reordering with buffers.

LFU evicts the key used least often, so you track a use count per key. The O(1) design: a map key to value and count, plus a map count to a LinkedHashSet of keys, and a variable minCount. On get or put, move the key from its count bucket to count + 1, and update minCount if the old bucket was empty. To evict, remove the oldest key from the minCount bucket. Example: counts a=3, b=1, c=1 evicts b (oldest among count 1). All operations are O(1) time, O(capacity) space.

Because it re-links the entry to the tail of the internal doubly linked list, which changes the structure. In access-order mode get(k) removes the node and appends it at the end, increasing modCount. So iterating while calling get on the same map throws ConcurrentModificationException, and two threads that call get at once can corrupt the links. This is why a read in an LRU cache needs a write lock. Insertion-order maps do not have this problem.

code.title: Simulating ArrayList growth and amortised cost

followUps: Doubling (2x) wastes more memory and is not much faster; 1.5x gives a better balance. With growth factor g, the total copy work is about n times g/(g-1): 2x gives about 2n copies and 1.5x about 3n, so 1.5x copies more but never wastes more than 33 percent of the array versus up to 50 percent. A factor under about 1.618 also lets freed old blocks be reused by later allocations. In the demo above, 1.5x copied 2.43 elements per add for 1,000,000 adds. It is a trade-off, not a law.

About 30 resizes for one million elements. Starting from capacity 10 and multiplying by 1.5 each time (with integer rounding), the capacity passes one million after 30 growth steps; the demo above ends at capacity 1,215,487. The check: 10 x 1.530 is roughly 1.9 million, and 1.528 x 10 is about 850,000. With new ArrayList<>(1_000_000) there are zero resizes. Total copying is a few million element moves, so it is cheap compared with creating the objects.

code.title: ConcurrentHashMap.merge across threads

followUps: No, check-then-act is not safe, even on ConcurrentHashMap. Two threads can both see containsKey false and then both put, so the second overwrites the first (a lost update). Each single call is atomic, but the pair is not. Use one atomic call: map.putIfAbsent(k, v) or map.computeIfAbsent(k, f). For counters use merge(k, 1, Integer::sum), as in the demo, which counted exactly 40,000 across 4 threads.

When the list is written often or is large. Every add, set or remove copies the whole array, which costs O(n) time and creates garbage. Example: 10,000 elements and 1,000 writes per second means copying about 10 million references per second, and each reader keeps an old copy alive. It is good only for small, read-mostly lists such as listener lists. For write-heavy cases use a ConcurrentLinkedQueue, a locked ArrayList or a different design.

code.title: Removing in a for-each: bug versus removeIf

followUps: Static tools flag it as a bug pattern, and you can enable them in CI. IntelliJ has an inspection "Collection is modified while iterating"; ErrorProne has ModifyCollectionInEnhancedForLoop; SpotBugs and IntelliJ also warn about the remove(int) versus remove(Object) confusion on a List of Integer. Exact rule names vary by version, so check yours. Make the build fail on those warnings so generated code that breaks the contract is blocked before review. Static tools only catch the obvious shape, so tests still matter.

Test a property that must hold for any input, not for a few chosen examples. For filter(list, pred): the result has only items that satisfy pred; its size is at most the input size; the order of kept items is unchanged; applying the filter twice equals applying it once; no input item satisfying pred is lost. A generator (jqwik, for example) creates thousands of random lists, including empty ones and ones with adjacent matches. Example: the buggy version fails on [1, 3, 4] almost at once. Shrinking then reports the smallest failing list.
